entries.before: A commercial property loan declined by a bank does not always mean the transaction is unworkable. It usually means the deal did not fit that bank's policy, servicing model, valuation view, asset appetite, lease requirements, or timing. Non-bank lenders and private credit providers may assess the same commercial property differently, but the file still needs a clear purpose, security position, repayment pathway, and risk story.
entries.after: A commercial property loan declined by a bank does not always mean the transaction is unworkable. Emet Capital is a broker, not a lender, and our [commercial property loan options](/services/commercial-property-finance) page explains how we compare bank and non-bank pathways.

entries.before: Commercial property LVR is the loan-to-value ratio a lender uses to compare proposed debt against the commercial property value it accepts for finance. In simple terms, it shows how much of the property value is being funded by debt and how much equity buffer remains in the deal.

entries.before: Bridge lending in Australia for commercial property is short-term, business-purpose finance used to bridge a timing gap between one property or funding event and another. In plain terms, it can help a business borrower settle, refinance, complete a sale, or protect a transaction while a longer-term funding source is being finalised.

In plain terms, it can help a business borrower settle, refinance, complete a sale, or protect a transaction while a longer-term funding source is being finalised. Emet Capital arranges [commercial bridging loans](/services/bridging-finance) as a broker, not as the lender.

entries.before: Bridging finance is short-term funding used to cover a timing gap between a purchase, refinance, sale, settlement, or other confirmed funding event. In Australia, business owners, property investors, and developers commonly use bridging finance when they need to complete a commercial property transaction before longer-term funds are available.
entries.after: Bridging finance is short-term funding used to cover a timing gap between a purchase, refinance, sale, settlement, or other confirmed funding event. In Australia, business owners, property investors, and developers commonly use bridging finance when they need to complete a commercial property transaction before longer-term funds are available. If you have a live timing gap, our [bridging finance service](/services/bridging-finance) explains what lenders will ask for.

entries.before: An open bridging loan is a short-term commercial facility where the exit date is expected but not fully locked in at settlement. A closed bridging loan is a short-term commercial facility where the repayment event is already defined, documented, and usually tied to a contracted sale or a refinance with a known completion path. That is the cleanest way to separate the two.
entries.after: An open bridging loan is a short-term commercial facility where the exit date is expected but not fully locked in at settlement. That is the cleanest way to separate the two. Either structure can be discussed through our [short-term bridging finance](/services/bridging-finance) page.

entries.before: Commercial bridging loans for property auctions are short-term commercial facilities used when an investor, developer, or business owner needs to settle an auction purchase before longer-term finance, a property sale, or another exit event is complete. The facility bridges a timing gap. It does not remove the need for due diligence, security, valuation, legal review, or a credible repayment plan.
